A baby can put his rosy little toe M his mouth more easily than his father can, but when it comes to putting the ! whole foot In it, the man of years and experience can die, count the baby half a hundred and then run out. If children are but echoes, "syllabling men's wonla," they are also alsorbent,, •ctively taking in all the induenem around theta. Them is a sacredness about the innocence of ! a child that makes its presence act like a check upon the frivolous and the cynical. The spirit in which all neekers after truth should look on the marvels of creation is well illustrated in this story,' which comm from an ancient boak added to one of the, Vedas, or weed booke of the Hindoos :—A father told his vain-minded son, in whom no aeries of wonder dwelt, to bring him • fruit of the huge banyan tree, or Indian fig-tree. , "Break it," said the father "what do you ~ee I" "Some very small weds," replied the eon. " Break one of them— , what do you see in it ?" asked the tither. "Nothing, my lather," answered the son. "My child," mid the father, where you see nothing, there dwells a mighty banyan- tree." Alma awn Lam Waren.—Milk and lime water 09 fre- • quently prescribed by physiciane in cases of dyepernm and , weakness of the stomach, and in some cases are said to prove very beneficial. Many persons who think good bread and milk a great luxury hesitate to eat it, for the reason that the milk will not digest readily ; sourness of st..mach will often follow. But experience provw that lime water and milk are not only food and medicine at an early period of life, but also at a later, when, an in the cane of infanm, di the functions of gestion and assimilation are feeble and easily perverted. A stomach taxed by gluttony, irritated by improper food, inflamed by dlcohol, enfeebled .by disease, or otherwise unfitted for its duties —an is shown by the vari- oue symptoms attendant upon indigestion, dyspepeia, diar- rhoea, dyeentery, and fever—will rmuine its work, and do it energetically, on an exclusive diet of bread and milk and lime water. What they could not reach, they might pull down with their crook. There still exist baundary stones. beyond which the "hook and crook folk" were not permitted to go. This custom, how. ever, is not generally regarded tu the origin of the phrase in question,! ,utgb some writers accept it aa ouch. John Amphlett in an article it the Gentlenwta'a Magarine says it is the roll or book in which an account is kept of the proceedings in the court of the manor to which any lands belong; and, to understand clearly their invention., we must consider a little how these courts arose, mid what they hall to deal with. Al the time of the Conquest the lands which were confiscated from the conquered Saxons were parcelled out by the Conqser, arnooget his followers, and in this way the greater part of the hods in the kingdom became the pomessions of the Norman soldiery. They were not, never- theless, given freely and for nothing; but tiny were given to hold of the Kink subject to the performance of certain military or other duties as the condition of their enjoy- ment ; and this feudal syetern of tenure wee applied soon after to those lands also which had not forrmol the subject of • grant, but remained in the hands of their coign.' /Saxon hollers. When a baron or great lord became thus possessed of a tract of loud, he nouslly resorvei come part of It for himself, which formed the demesnes of the manor ; part of it he granted to freemen as estates in fe—sintple, to be held lor various kinds of tenure, and part of it he granted out to his villeins or slaves, permitting them, as an act of pure fav,mr. to enjoy such lands at hi, pleasure; while, if any toed remaintd, it became waste land of the manor, over which the tenants enjoyed rights of cemtnon. Thus arose a manor, of which the tenants formed two clam, the freeholders and the villeins. E tell manor powered a jurisdiction called a Court Baron in flee case of the freeholders, or a Customary Court when it ru, held fur the villeins, at which IMP tran,aeled all th • public business of the manor. Each manor now usually forme a parieh or part of • parish; but while within the limits al one pariah there may be several manors, it is very uncommon for one manor to contain several parishes or parts of ptrishen, on- less they are of quite recent erection. The privileges granted to the villein. were, for the most part, eufferen to remain to their children and in courm of Bine common law gave these tenants a right to hold against their font if the services of their tenure were duly porformed noel the customs of the manor properly observed Though they were mid to be tenants at the will of the lord, it must be such swill as if agreeable to the ciatoms of the manor. These customs. if they were not kept on foot by immono- riel usage, were preserved and kept in evidence hy the records or tells of the several Courts Baron in which they were entered cud,,, the tenants hail nothing to show for their lands hut these cost.. and admissions in accordance with them, they came tn her dist ten Int, by ropy of Court Roll, and their tenure itself e coprhold. In the reign of Edward IV. the Judges gave to copyholders • certainty of tenure, by allowing them en action for trespass against their lords if they attempted to eject them without just cause. Now," my, Sir Edward Coke, ° copyhelders stand upon • Imre ground ; now they weigh not their lord's displeasure ; they shake Ilot at every blast of wed; they eat, drink, and sleep securely, only having a special care of the Inain chance, namely, to perform carefully what duties and ser- vices soever their tenure doth exact and custom dotb require; then let lords frown. the copyholder cares nots knowing himself safe." Thus, a copyholder cone to have as good a title as • freeholder tor all the transaetions relating to the conveyance of cop,4toldeie wet, entered on the Court Rolla of the manor, and thus a record was p • -ed of the titlee of all the tenants.

Obey Hole is a celebrated natural cavern of England, on the south side of Mendip hills. The entrance is in the fall of Mow hills, beset all about with rocks, and ham near it • precipitate rt.:scent of nearly twelve fathoms deep, at the bottom of which there continually issues from the rocks a considerable current of water. The naked rocks above the entrance are about thirty fathoms high, and the whole ascent of the hill above is about a mile, and very steep. A. you pass into this voult, you go first upon a level; but, ad- vancing farther, the way in rocky and uneven, nometimes ucentling, and sometimes descending. The roof of this Cavern, in llm highest part, is about eight fathoms from the ground, bat in many places it is no low that one must stoop to get aleng. The breadth is not lees various than the height, for in some places it is five or six forborne wide, and in others not more than one or two. It is in length algut 203 yarde. At the farthest part of the cavern there is a stream ef ware, large enough to drive a mill, which pawn all along one side of the cavern, and at length elides down about six or eight fathoms among the rocks and then, pres- sing through the clefts, falls into the valley. The river within the cavern is well stored with eels, and has some route looter summers a great numb, of frogs Cr, seen all along this cavern, even to the farthest part of it; and on the root ate Cat numbers of bans. (Tittering in court.) After waiting sometime, thinking that the guard which the women had mounted, had got disheartened, the defendant left the place, I but lie found that the watchers were still there. They epoke to him, and he went away, hiding his head art a nom would and ought to do under such circumstances, and mot attempt- ing to give any explanation of why he wee on the premien. at that time etch, night. aam toe Bible Society _ _ more honourable one thin the ill u.trious title sabre!. graced hie name or the coronet which encircled hie brow. He was , glad to tied the extent to which the young people connected with their churches had leen enlisted in forwa.liog the work of the Christian missions in connection with the Run- corn circuit. He thought if anything they hyl done more than their elders. (Hear, hear.) He briefly sp,ke in support of the idea th lit was reationabletomppow that the en--min of Christ were always to ha the most numeroue on the earth, but that His followers would in titne form a great majority. Celeee he misread the signs of the times, he had • definite conviction that the work of salvation would by and by proceed with wonder( ul majesty and power. anti on a male of grandeur of which their stunted faith could hardly form any conception. Mobarninedism had had its day of power, heathenism had had its day of power, Popery had had its age of power, ignorance, barbariem, superstition, and idolatry had had their thy of rule and p wee, and a dark day for the world it hat been, but now the time had cone for the fair f ice of truth to be shown. When they looked beyond-their own boundary, as a cmnezion, at the work which was being done by the universal church, they saw all the might and power of the world to be Christian. False religions were breaking aad crumbling to dust through sheer exhaust'on and imbecility. They had unlimited accessibility to all the great seats and centres of the warld'e population. India. China, JApen, aria. and Africa were open to them, and they had the Word of God translated into almoet all the languages of the earth. It was impossible by any numerical formula to show the way in which old forms Aere dying out The disin- tegrationbelw the surface all false nstems of philosophy and religion, and the growing up of • new eystem, 000 w spirit of life going out amongst men, brooding with energy upon the etegnant bosom of society, and kindling new hopes and aspirations. The great powers of this world were all silent powers. It seas said that the rush of God's omnipo- tence never net disturbed the slumbers of an infant. The speed of • cannon ball was nothing to the speed of light, yet how gently it struck upon the eye. What wae the breath of spring! Something ethereal. Tom/ saw the ex- I istence of a mighty mysterious force which they ix uld not I confine, bet which worked noiselessly, unseen in every bough above their heads and in blade of grass beneani their feet. What a complicated Mechanism was that of I nature! Ever garlanding the earth with new beauty and , glory and covering the world with forms of lovelier.; yet there was no jar whilst all this work was being done. The dew fell softly. Nobody saw it, nobody heard it. None marked the process. Sual was the subtlety and the mystery of the operation that to some it was a doubtful question whether it was distilled from above or exhaled from be- neath. How quietly the day broke. The sun dial not burst upon the horizon and come upon them immediately with his imperial splendour, but, liked monarch preceded by his herald to announce his approach, he threw open the door of his chamber, the glad earth gave him her welcome, nature doffed her sable mantle and woke up to pay her morning homage, until he rose higher and higher in the heavens and mounted his throne. As it was in the phyeical world so it was in the moral world. In spiritual life there were spring times with their magic Much and fertilising power. There were times of disenthrallment and renovation when old tnings passed away and all things become new, when the breath of heaven was abroad animating tke smile of tuen. when the elomber of ages was breaking and men started from their spiritual death and maved up to • higher platform, being filled with a purer faith, a nobler hope. and a clo.er I walk with God and yet they could not put such things down in a book or tabulate them. Then. as Methodism. were too deeirone of quick returns. whereas it would Ix much water for them if they would study the method in which nature worked, which was not by rapid changes
with the Bibl;Sociel!

hut by silent growth. It behoved them to de this if they ' would escape bitter disappointment. They must remember that Every hill shall be made low, every valley shall las exalted, the rough places shall be mole plain.- before the , glory of the Lord could be revealed. They were so &nab.= for, great work that they ii;er, inclined to think that stead• ' progress wae hardly worth recording, but preparation via ...en; contending with difficulties was success: and the very commotion. which were generated in the world by the , contact with truth were elements of Puttees. ( Applause • The Rev. Z /MCI Rolm:sox spoke at some length on his work in South and bouth-Eastem Africa. It the former ' colony he spent nearly 13 years, mid in the latter—that was in Natal—seven years of his ministerial life. He referred to the labours of William Shaw, a famous missionary in the district, and showed how, during the last ell years, the work ad creating • Christian sentiment in the ' community had progremel in a marvellous man- ner. until it even innuenced the members of the mirage Inlet, He considered that to this was due the fact that to, the late war Cetewayo did not descend upon the colonists , with his army before the Arrival of the British reinforce- ments. and carry; fire and sward through the entire settle- ; : went, AA he might, without a doubt, have done. fir,—Will you permit me through the medium of your columns, to call Attention ton most remarkable presage of history aenarrated by Mr. Alderman Kean. There are some other strange re- fiections, hut I fancy the first aentence in incomparable for the blundering misstatements it contains. Now, if Macaulay's favourite achoolboy be yet alive, he would tell Mr. Kean that William 111. was the lame oft marriage of Charles i.e daughter Mary (horn 11131) with the Prince of Orange. The newt reference in the same nentence is equally fine i• its way. It would have henna beget wonder than any of" the great wonders in the land" King William was to work, had the people of England rejoiced at the birth of title wonderful personage ; because, when William was teltered into the world, his chance of succeeding to the English mown meet. remote as such a thing could be, Charles It. being then a young man of twenty, and the Duke of York, afterwanls Jame. it,. youth of seventeen. THE STATE OF IRELAND. CAPTAIN BOYCOTT AND HIS CROPS.,

The party of Northern lalmurers who arrived at Captain &rotes fern on Friday in order to harvest his Crops began work on Saturday morning, a strong police wort eurroand- lag them while working, whiled a cavalry vedette and police- man were etatiooml all around. Owing to the violence of lila weather, however, the relieving party were compelled to cease working at one o'clock. A few of the neighbouring peaeantry stood at a distance watching their operations, but there was no demonstration, and everything so far has .:doff quietly. The cost of keeping and feeding each • eircert of policemen, military, and workers on his (acre wil Is considerable, and to all appearance what portions of Captain Boycott'a cropa have been spared lip the weather Will be eaten up by the friends who have come to relieve him. Owing to the imperfect coTntnissariatlrrangementa of the military, the soldiers have had to fall hack upon the resources of the farm, and on Friday evening they devoured at finer *an forty-two of Captain Boycott's eheep, beside. Making oonehieral;le depndations in his poultry yard. Con- sidering tho surroundings at his present position, it teen wander that Captain Boycott intends to leave the neighbour- hood immediately his crops are housed. Stories of Captain Boycott's unpopularity continue to some across the channel. One of the relief contingent, des- cribing the arrival of the coluinn at Lough !Bask, says that when thy entered the Rome leading to Captain Boycott's house the captain gesed at them with whet appeared like indifference, and gave them no welcome. Cheers were called for Captain Boycott, but no responses wae given. This would not have been wonderful had the relief party been aware that after their long march no dinner had hem pro- rided for them. They were not, however, supposed to know this, hots fact, nevertheless, it was, and the men had to be content with coffee and biscuits, after which they were ordered to bed. Ugly gorier, were circulated about the way in which Captain Boycott treated the tenantry, and the cor- respondent we are quoting from was informed that the cap- ' tain had frequently tined his labourere for standing up to reet themselves when working, that he fined them the full price of implements broken or mining, and even fined his tenants if their hens trespassed on hit ground. Altogether, if this cortespondent's information is to be relied upon, Captain Boycott does not seem the man for whom anyone would run the risk of being shot at from behind a hedge, I but then it must be rtmembared that the correspondent in question took his first impressions of Captain Boycott on a hungry etomach—a condition al things apt to engender per- Islet way or the other. . . . .

Affairs hove assumed 000 W and term -serious pliare on Lord Erne'. Mayo estates. Ihe tenant farmers are about to Agitate in a somewhat more constitutional fashion for the removal of Captain Boycott, their unpopular agent, rinfl,! copying the Ulster •• roliof expedition," propose to send a I deputation to wait personally on Lord Erne, tendering lam their full rents, and praying-fora new agent. The propowd I deputation will he quite of a friendly character, and will not rerreire an army of soldiere for it, protection. Those who have suggeMed this more have very small hopes, pro- bably, of persuading Lord Erne to throw over the man who hoe undergone so much prosecution in his eerviorl but the real end in view 101 be Attained if the tenant farmers of Mayo cm show tbc people of 111-ten by their preceable in- vasion "of Fermanagh, where Loot Erne lives, that they know how to agitate withoLl breaking tho law. The Land League has hitherto !wen in htil odur with the L'lster farmers for reasorm which are obvious. and which it is now sought to remove. Captain Boycott had on Trienlay to go in .earth et hie docks and herds, which bed boon maliciously driven from. farm of hie some miles from Lough Mark He had, of course, to So escorted by sot tiers, and his 'Manion being bighty succeseful the singular picture W. shortly presented of a troop of cavalry commanded Ly a colonel moving along the tares of Mayo in the rOle of cattle drovers. Toe Ulster iovaition" of Mayo is likely to end M all but a complete fiLOOO, MOSI of the hand who 30 gallantly reat out for Captain Boycott's "relief " being thoroughly dirturged with their self-imposed task. Their treatment hoe been none of the best, and their sympathies have been enlisted on the side of the tenantry. The mortification among the Ulmer Tories who got up thie grand eemi-political demonstration for purposts of their own is now bitter in the extreme. Several of those who, at much trouble and expenee, and at. great risk to the country, were sent to the West to vindicate territorialism, have been talking of joinleg (be deputation of tenantry which wae this week to "invade " Meter for the ptirposa of laying their grievances before ford From, awl petitioning the the dismissal of Captain Boycott, who seems to bare failed ao signally in his relations with the "relief ' expedition " It ie reported, however, thalthis latter expedi- ! lion will not be carried out.
